title: How Do Headphones Cancel Noise With More Noise?
description:
Noise-cancelling headphones don't block the engine roar. They add a second sound: its mirror image, so the two cancel at your ear.
Here is how that works, and why it tames the low drone of a plane but barely touches the voice next to you.

subtitles: How can a pair of headphones make the world quieter by adding more noise?
Put on noise-cancelling headphones on a plane and press one button.
The low roar of the cabin drops sharply.
But pressing the button blocked nothing new.
The headphones did not get thicker.
They started making sound.
Most people think noise cancelling works like a wall, keeping sound out.
It doesn't.
It fights sound with sound.
By the end of this video, you will know why it tames the low drone of a plane.
And why it barely touches the voice of the person next to you.
Start with what sound actually is.
When an engine roars, it pushes the air.
That push travels outward as a pattern of squeezed air and stretched air, one after the other.
When it reaches your ear, the squeezes push your eardrum in.
The stretches pull it out.
Draw that pressure over time and you get a wave.
High points are squeezes.
Low points are stretches.
How tall the wave is sets how loud it is.
How often it repeats sets the pitch.
A deep engine hum repeats about 100 times a second.
A whistle, a few thousand.
Now here is the trick.
Imagine the noise squeezes the air at your ear.
At that exact moment, a tiny speaker stretches it by the same amount.
The squeeze and the stretch meet, and they add up to nothing.
The air at your eardrum barely moves.
Two waves, each loud on its own, together make silence.
Physicists call this destructive interference.
The second wave is a mirror image of the first: every peak where the noise has a trough.
It is the same reason two ripples on a pond can meet and leave a patch of flat water.
So noise-cancelling headphones are really tiny, very fast mirror makers.
Open one up and you find three things.
A microphone on the outside listens to the world before the sound reaches you.
A chip works out the mirror image of that sound.
And the speaker that plays your music also plays that mirror image, mixed in.
Many headphones add a second microphone inside the ear cup.
It hears what actually reached your ear, and corrects whatever the first one missed.
This idea is surprisingly old.
A German inventor, Paul Lueg, patented it in the 1930s.
But it took decades of faster electronics before it fit on your head.
Bose sold noise-cancelling headsets to pilots in the late 1980s.
Ordinary travellers got them much later.
So why did it take so long?
Because the mirror has to be almost perfect.
Imagine the anti-noise arrives a little late.
Now its stretch no longer lines up with the noise's squeeze.
Part of the noise leaks through.
Arrive half a cycle late, and the two waves line up peak with peak.
Instead of silence, you have made the wave twice as tall: louder, not quieter.
To cut the sound's energy by 99%, the timing must be right to about a sixtieth of a cycle.
For a 100-hertz engine hum, a cycle lasts 10 milliseconds.
A sixtieth of that is about a sixth of a millisecond.
That leaves room for small errors.
For a sound at 2,000 hertz, a cycle lasts half a millisecond.
Now the whole system, fit included, must be accurate to about 8 millionths of a second.
So the higher the pitch, the harder the mirror is to get right.
And there is a second problem: space.
Cancellation does not happen everywhere.
It only works in a small bubble around the point where the two waves match.
Acousticians have worked out that bubble for sound arriving from all around in a room.
Where the sound energy drops ten-fold, it is only about a tenth of a wavelength across.
A 100-hertz hum has a wavelength of about 3.5 metres.
A tenth of that is 34 centimetres, wider than your whole head.
Easy.
The bubble swallows your ear.
But a sound at 3,000 hertz has a wavelength of about 11 centimetres.
Its quiet bubble is about one centimetre wide.
The inner microphone sits a few centimetres from your eardrum.
At that pitch, that is already outside the bubble.
So the quiet zone shrinks as the pitch rises.
Put the two problems together, and you get the answer to our puzzle.
Engine roar, air conditioning, train rumble: low, steady, predictable.
The headphones cancel them beautifully.
Voices are higher, and they change every fraction of a second.
The mirror can never quite keep up.
So for high sounds, headphones fall back on the oldest trick of all.
Thick, soft padding simply blocks them.
Active cancelling handles the low end.
Padding handles the high end.
Together they make the quiet you hear.
Think about the noisiest place you sit every week.
Is its noise a low rumble, or a high chatter?
Now you know which one your headphones will win against.
So, how can headphones cancel noise with more noise?
They listen to the world and build its mirror image.
They play it into your ear at exactly the right moment.
The squeeze and the stretch meet, and add up to almost nothing.
The lower and steadier the sound, the better the mirror works.
That is why the jet engine fades, and the voice beside you fades much less.
Here, quiet is not the absence of sound waves.
It is two waves perfectly out of step, right at your ear.
